utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, Judge Riad. We are going to move back to the cross-examination of Mr. Vulliamy that we postponed, I believe, on the 24th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe the Defence counsel has the floor and if the usher could bring Mr. Vulliamy into the courtroom? (The witness entered court). WITNESS; Resumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, good morning. Thank you for coming again. You hear me? Thank you for coming. You are still under oath. I will not repeat to explain the conditions under which we're meeting today, but for you, that doesn't change anything at all. You will be asked questions by Defence counsel. This will not change anything in terms of your examination-in-chief and cross-examination. It is a procedural issue that has been resolved in full agreement between the Prosecution and the Defence to sit in the absence of one judge; whereas, the two Judges, Judge Riad and myself, have been designated as presiding officers. So nothing is changing. You're still under oath. You will now be asked questions by Mr. Hayman, one of the Defence counsel of General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, first, is it correct that you testified for the Office of the Tribunal Prosecutor in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you agreed to testify in future cases in the future, without identifying the cases; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've been notified that there's likely to be one other, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to that portion of your testimony on direct examination which dealt with your meeting with Mate Boban on the 13th of August 1992. With the permission of the court, if at any time you would like to refer to a transcript of the your earlier testimony, the Defence would certainly encourage you to ask for that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do have one, not with me now, but I'll do my best not to waste your time. I do have the same notes I had with me last time. I'll refer to them and save you the bother, if possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. Do you recall at your meeting with Mate Boban on 13 August, 1992, was there anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was, a reporter from the Associated Press with whom I had been to the AMP (phoen) at Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can you just look at us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I'm sorry, yes, forgive me. --- Short pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. We have a problem with the transcript. You testify in many of the hearings, then you are a witness to many of the troubles that we are having with the equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's quite all right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For you, in the end. Now, it's working. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, who was the AP reporter who was present with you in that meeting on 13th August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her name was Maude Bielmann from the AP and there was a translator who was employed by the Associated Press whose name, I'm afraid, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in that meeting, Mate Boban voiced support for a federal system of government in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted a form of government that he called that of cantons or provinces. I don't recall the word "federal" being used, but, I mean, the bit that I noted and that stuck in my mind was this reference to cantons and provinces and that he was talking about his difficulties in accepting the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina as formulated when it secured its independence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that at no time in the meeting he stated that Herceg-Bosna should legally become a part of Croatia; that is, be annexed to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He didn't use the term annexed. To the best of my recollection the term -- the term was that Herceg-Bosna was culturally, spiritually and economically part of Croatia but had been severed from Croatia by what he called unfortunate historical circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree at no time did he state that Herceg-Bosna should legally become a part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall him using the word "legally," but it was fairly clear that he didn't intend for there to be much of a border between the two. Indeed, there wasn't at the time, a fairly cursory border, anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may pause for a moment after your answers to allow the interpreters to complete their interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for your information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me direct your attention to Travnik. In September of 1992, at about that time, were there refugees coming into Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, thousands of refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly from the area around Prijedor, Samski Most, Banja Luka, and the north-western Bosnian Krajina as it's called, and they were coming over the road, a road which I knew well. A part of my testimony before did not cover, because it wasn't directly relevant, an occasion on which -- whereas a correspondent from Reuters I joined one of these convoys which the Serbs were herding over the mountains throughout a no-man's land at a place called Smet. They were pretty terrifying convoys and they were coming down into Travnik throughout August when I travelled on one, and throughout September and, indeed, into the autumn, they continued to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In September when you travelled with this group of refugees, were the refugees predominantly Croat on Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Predominantly Muslim, but there were some Croats among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an estimate whether there was 1,000 or 5,000 refugees on this occasion in September, 1992 that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, the number that had come into Travnik - this is to the best of my recollection - when I made that journey in August, 1992 was something like 36- to 40,000 had come over that road from the Prijedor area, and by the time I went back in September, although it might have been at a slightly later date, I recall the figure of 76,000, yes. So we're talking about tens of thousands, yes. During the time I was in Travnik in September, it would have been two nights' worth, as it were, and I think that probably from my experience the convoy I was on would have represented some 2- to 3,000 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that those numbers were larger than the size of towns such as Travnik and Vitez? Do you know how large Travnik was, perhaps I should ask first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, I'm afraid, because the population was impossible to gauge. All I know is the number of refugees swelling, the original populations of Travnik and Vitez became proportionately higher and higher as the autumn went on, obviously, yes. They moved some on to Zenica and to Herzegovina, depending on their origin, but most had to stay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that these vast numbers of refugees moving into Bosnia were severely overtaxing the infrastructure and social services available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, such as they were. People were doing the best job they could to cope, but, I mean, there wasn't much of an infrastructure to tax. But obviously the authorities in both Travnik and Vitez and other towns, Zenica in particular, were finding it difficult to cope with these numbers, yeah, particularly since these towns -- or Travnik was still under siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your earlier examination that in September of '92 you met an HVO commander in Travnik by the name of Pokrajcic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Joko Pokrajcic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he said "he was not going to bow to pressure from either side", quote, unquote, page 7758 of the transcript. Did he say to you who or what forces were specifically putting pressure on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, he made it clear that he was talking about his own army, on the one hand, putting pressure on him to be part of a hostile state of affairs with the Muslims, and that there was pressure on him from the Muslim side too, and that he was resisting this pressure. In fact, he said, his words, to the best of my recollection were: "I'm here to fight for the victim peoples of this war", and said something about "over my dead body will I not do that".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say specifically to you, though, who was putting such pressure on him on the Croat or HVO side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't name any names, no, but he -- I mean, he left room for no other inference than, I'm caught between these two sets of pressures and that on the Croat side it was coming from his own army, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did he say -- I take it he said nothing more, whether there was pressure from Mostar, pressure from local politicians, pressure from the regional command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't specify on that occasion, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let me direct your attention to the next month, October of 1992. You said you heard that on October 20th, 1992 Mate Boban had visited Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the paper when we were in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Slobodna Dalmacija, but I don't, I'm afraid, no. It could have been one of the Croatian papers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, was it a Croatian language paper or an English language paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you read the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't, but we had translators reading the papers for us every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to anyone in Travnik that said they had seen Mate Boban in Travnik in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anybody in Travnik, but I talked to people at the Vitez radio station about it, yes. That would be the following night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say about Boban, whether or not he had been in Travnik in October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They confirmed that he had been, but we didn't talk about it much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you heard that on the 21st of October, 1992, there was a shoot-out or a conflict at a gas station over the division of petroleum supplies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all from my translator, who is also a cameraman, and then later when we got up to Vitez, at the radio station people were talking about it, both the Muslim and the Croatian people at the radio debate were talking about this incident at the gas station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of those people tell you who had attacked whom in connection with this gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The account I heard from the guy who was producing the programme was that there had been an argument over the distribution of fuel and that the HVO had said to the Muslim that they weren't going to get their share or their entire share, and there was an argument and an exchange of fire and a Muslim was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a local history; that is, a history within Travnik going back some time concerning a dispute over this gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I knew that there had been -- I mean, when I went back in September, that's when I very first heard about, shall we say, arguments or tensions that Mr. Pokrajcic, that we spoke about earlier that we dealt with, but I didn't know until that day that there was a particular dispute about fuel, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn whether or not there was, though, a history at the local level going back many months to this dispute that ultimately erupted into violence over this gasoline station in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about a dispute over that specific gasoline station up until that night, no. A dispute over an arms factory in the area, yes, but not the gas station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during your direct testimony that also in October of 1992 you heard a radio station, a radio programme involving Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. No, I was actually at -- this was actually the same radio forum in a house in Vitez where the station was based and he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were present and you heard the dialogue and discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were sitting in the room where they were having the dialogue, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said in the course of that discussion Pero Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak said that the HVO was the only legal authority in Vitez, or something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from now on was the gist of what he was saying, but it was a declaration of what he seemed to think was the new state of affairs in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Pero Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was representing the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he representing civilian elements; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't. He was introduced as being the -- representing the HVO. This debate, this forum, call it what you will, the HDZ was represented, the HVO was represented, the Muslim party, the SDA was represented as was the Bos -- actually, no, the Bosnian army were not, and he was the representative of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone present at this forum, as you put it, in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, everyone was in civilian clothes, except for some of the aids who were sort of hanging about at the back and the people guarding the doors and so on. But the debaters, if you like, the participants were in civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said during your testimony on page 7766 that you heard an ultimatum had been issued in Mostar by the HVO to the Bosnian army that it was to disarm immediately and either disband or come under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued that so-called ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO in Mostar. It was on the radio in Split when we returned from Novi Travnik that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether it was issued by a local command, national; that is, Herceg-Bosna HVO command or some other element within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it had certainly been issued by the HVO in Mostar as we found out when we got there, but given what we had just heard in Vitez and what we had seen in Novi Travnik and what I had heard from Mr. Boban and would hear from Mr. Boban within 36 hours, it seemed to be coming from everywhere, from the top.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't recall you saying that in Vitez Pero Skopljak had taken the position that the BiH army had to disarm immediately and come under HVO command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't say that--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any such statement in this radio discussion programme that you observed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall the details about disarming, but he did say that the HVO was the only legal authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you seem to have quite a good memory. Did he issue an ultimatum that was equivalent to the ultimatum you learned of on 23rd October, 1992 having been issued, you have testified, by the HVO in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall him making that specific ultimatum about disarming, no, but I have a note of him saying that the HVO was the only legal authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the so-called ultimatum you learned of in Mostar was directed to the BiH army in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was directed at the BiH army right across the territory. I mean, it was being directed at them in Mostar through that -- in that specific language, but, I mean, all over the territory the HVO was taking over in the areas that it claimed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in what way was this ultimatum issued to the BiH army in Busovaca, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't in Busovaca, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way was this ultimatum issued within the municipality of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kiseljak, I don't know. The BiH army was insignificant in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you slow down for the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would later see it being enforced, not verbally, but in armed action within 48 hours of Mostar in Prozor, Tomislavgrad and so on. So, yes, it was across the board. I mean, I wasn't in every town to hear the ultimatum being made verbally. I'm not claiming that. What I'm saying is that the HVO was described as "the only legal authority in Vitez," as the fighting started there. As fast as one could keep up, it was happening in Mostar and then -- well, I won't jump the gun, but I've testified as to what happened in Prozor after that, which was most articulate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Aside from the radio discussion programme involving Pero Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak Skopljak whom you were not able to identify as a civilian or a military figure, do you have any other information confirming that any ultimatum of any sort was issued to the BiH army in the Vitez municipality on or about 23 October, 1992 telling the BiH army has had that it had to immediately disarm or come under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've described that situation in the radio debate to the best of my recollection and as far as my notes back up that recollection. As regards to Mr. Skopljak, I'm saying that he represented the HVO. I think he was in civilian uniform, civilian clothes, sorry. But as regards ultimatum in Vitez, those are the words I took note of and I think one can say that firing a substantial amount of ammunition into the Muslim enclave in the centre of the town is a fairly articulate declaration of intent. There was a lot of shooting going on as well as radio talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that there was -- that you were told that there were barricades, BiH army barricades in Stari Vitez and shooting both coming out and going into Stari Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was told that the Muslims in Stari Vitez had put up barricades, I have no reason to disbelieve that and the shooting was going both ways, but I think I've made it clear that most of the shooting seemed to be, as we could ascertain - which is not to the point of certainty - going in, rather than out of the Muslim area. But, most importantly, I testified and would do so again, that the mobilisation around Vitez was a very substantial one and that all the roadblocks that we went through coming up to Vitez and leaving the following day were HVO and the troops coming up the line, as I put it before, were HVO. I mean, this was not a sort of an isolated event. There was a very substantial mobilisation going on by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described the conflicts that you saw or heard about in Travnik, Vitez, and the ultimata -- one or more ultimata in Mostar in October, 1992 as an all-out war, page 7765 of the transcript. In your view, did an all-out war start in October, 1992 between the HVO and the BiH army and continue thereafter until the Washington Agreement; is that your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we -- well, I tried to sort of -- I mean, we tried to tell us that this can't be a war, these people are allies. What I saw in Prozor a couple of days after going to Mostar was an all-out war, not between the HVO and the BiH army, but between the HVO and the civilian -- the Muslim civilians of Prozor, who, as I testified before, were shelled and gunned out of town. Certainly by the time we get to the Washington Agreement, there was an all-out war being waged against the civilians of east Mostar, that's for sure. Your point that this was continuous is, I mean, is a fair one. There were cease-fires here, cease-fires there, but the thrust was a war, yes, from that week -- the week beginning 20th or so of October through until the end of the siege in east Mostar that I described was, yes, an all-out war. It certainly wasn't a game of chess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that war came to Travnik in June of 1993, Mr. Vulliamy; real war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Within Travnik. Travnik was at war throughout, as you know, against the Serbs, but the war within Travnik between the Muslims and the Croats, summer of '93, yeah, maybe a little bit before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me. I want to be a little bit clear. When you spoke of the war between the 28th of October and the siege of east Mostar, is it war with civilians or war-war. The word 'war' has got a meaning. Please use the right words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and it is one that we grappled with throughout. I mean, a war one used to think of between armies, rival armies who fight by sort of mutual agreement. Very little of what happened in Bosnia between the Muslims and the Croats or the Serbs and the Muslims and Croats can be really described as war like that. The vast majority of the violence was by soldiers against civilians, and the vast majority of those killed and wounded were civilians, with the exception of some disastrous offensives in various directions. So, yeah, I'm glad you raised that, because I mean, one searches and continues to search for another word, but--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can it be called massacre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think shelling women and children in streets and houses - and I must not get too angry about this in a courtroom - it isn't war, it's something worse than war and 'worse than war' is a phrase I've used quite a lot. In the conflict that counsel is asking me about, yes, there were -- between the Muslims and the Croats and between October the 20th and February, '94, there were battles, if you like, between soldiers and exchanges of gunfire between soldiers. But most of the violence, most of the cruelty, most of the atrocities were by artillery, mortar, gunfire against civilians. That was the flavour, the tenor of this war and everything that happened in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Fighting civilians? Were they fighting back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. I mean, the pattern mostly was small communities under siege and you can't fight back. If I can summarise it - this could be a long answer - but to summarise, most of the violence was by -- was either shelling from hilltops into communities and death by sniper and motor fire, and occasional massacres as militias would go into communities and kill people as at -- well, Bosanska, Krupa, Zepa, Ahmici indeed when civilians were simply killed at close range. And then there were also -- there was violence against refugees. The convoy that I went on that I was talking about earlier when counsel asked me about the refugees, when we walked on that road to Travnik from Prijedor, there were bodies on the road. They were clearly shooting at refugees, that's the Serbs at that time. But certainly this was a war against civilians. We like to use the term 'refugee' meaning a side effect of war between armies, but in this conflict, the refugees were the raw material of the war, they were its whole point; the removal of populations was what the war was all about. They were the raison d’être, they weren't a side effect. The violence was against the civilians in the most part, and I use the word 'war' as shorthand. You're right, it is not strictly correct, it is war against people who have not the means to fight back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to the Prozor conflict in a moment. Staying with Travnik for just a question or two, would you agree that what you learned of and saw in Travnik in October, 1992 was not a conflict between the HVO and the civilians; it was a conflict between the HVO and the BiH army over material and military supplies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, absolutely. In Travnik, there was no war by the HVO against the Muslim civilians and there was no war by the Bosnian army against Croatian civilians. Travnik, the inter-necine war in Travnik -- sorry this is so complicated -- the internecine war in Travnik was actually a row between soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come to Prozor, let me ask you about your meeting again with Mate Boban on the 24th of October, 1992. You have told us, page 7772 of the transcript, that Mate Boban told you in this meeting, we have our political platform and anyone who disagrees with it will either step down or leave in some other manner. Did you understand him to be referring to officials or members of the HDZ party in Bosnia-Herzegovina stepping down if they did not agree with his platform when he made that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood him to mean anyone who didn't agree with him and his platform, be they in the HDZ or the HVO or any other grouping on the Croatian side - and I think I was right to infer that. The HVO and the HDZ are so entwined at this point that it seemed to be slicing a hair to make any distinction between them. He was saying, you know, this is the line, obey it, or else you're out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the HVO originally formed as the military wing of the HDZ party? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was formed as a Croatian army within Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the relationship between the HVO and the HDZ became, as I said, progressively entwined as the war went on. I don't think there's much debate about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the term 'someone stepping down if they don't agree with a political platform' appears to refer to politics and to a political party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as the commander Lacic, the commander of the HVO in Mostar had said to us that same afternoon, he had used the term civilian military authority. In these circumstances, there was no great distinction between a political project and the military one. Mr. Boban had articulated his political aims and had left us in no doubt that it was for the HVO to impose those aims militarily. I mean this wasn't an election manifesto.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with Mate Boban on 24 October, 1992, again, did he state that he believed Herceg-Bosna should legally become a part of Croatia,; that is, should be annexed to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't use the term legally, not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the conflict you witnessed or the aftermath of the conflict in Prozor, which I believe you witnessed on the 27th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I witnessed the aftermath on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say you arrived after whatever active fighting or firing had occurred was over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the conflict in Prozor broke out after a conflict between the HVO and the BiH army over the control of the road through Prozor to central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I can imagine that -- I certainly could accept that as an explanation. I tried to explain how important the road was to the HVO for reasons of controlling the aid to central Bosnia and also into Sarajevo for a lot of the time, and I can imagine that would have been of concern to anyone who wasn't in the HVO. But as you said, by the time we got there, the fighting, if that's the right word -- and again, I qualify that, given what I was asked from the Bench just now -- the shelling and the shooting of the civilians had finished because the Muslim civilians had all gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement with respect to Prozor that, as dawn broke, this is page 222 of your book, 'then as dawn broke and people started to flee, mobs had moved into town firing willy-nilly, and then began to torch, loot, and cleanse the town'?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would. That is what the people who we found next day in flight across the mountains told us, that the firing from the mountainside to the south-west of the town happened overnight, and at dawn these people came in and they were shooting everywhere and they started looting and burning the houses. Yes, that's what I was told and I hadn't seen anything in the town the previous day that suggested they were wrong. In fact, it seemed to be exactly right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you agree with the statement in your book on that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If the Registrar could assist and place Exhibit 29L on the ELMO, please? The easel, excuse me. I misspoke. Mr. Vulliamy, so we can collectively refresh our recollections, Exhibit 29L is a map of certain portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina on which you were kind enough, I believe, during your direct examination to indicate a route known as Route Diamond for aid coming from the south up into central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you testified at page 7780 of the transcript that it was militarily obvious that the HVO needed to control Prozor in order to secure a resupply route for troops and material in central Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that, do you mean it was a matter of military necessity for the HVO to preserve that resupply route into central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The UN troops were turning a mountain track into a fairly decent road so that they could take aid up into central Bosnia and, for awhile, also that route was necessary to supply Sarajevo as well, because the two tarmac routes in, one through Mostar, one through Livno were too dangerous because they were exposed to the Serb guns. My point was that for the HVO the Route Diamond had two functions -- well, control of the Route Diamond had two functions; one was because if you controlled it you controlled the supply of aid; and also, as was becoming clearer and clearer to them and they made no secret of this, it was a way for them to get their troops up into central Bosnia which you could see them doing day in and day out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without that route, the HVO in the Vitez and Busovaca municipalities were cut off by any outside resupply by land; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other routes would have been much more difficult, put it that way, yeah. The UN was building a road for them so obviously it was by the most convenient. There was another route that I did indicate that went up through Tarcin and up through Kiseljak, but that became too dangerous periodically, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, is it true that that route required you to be able to travel from Kiseljak to Busovaca on the road connecting those two towns in order to get to the Lasva or Busovaca municipalities -- excuse me, the Vitez or Busovaca municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Tarcin route, if you wanted to get to Vitez via Tarcin you would have to have gone through Busovaca, yes, which for the HVO presented problems because that was cut from their point of view for a while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was cut by the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO control Prozor from roughly October 27, 1992 until the signing of the Washington Accord?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, yes, and it still does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were the ability to block humanitarian aid going into central Bosnia, at least into the Vitez and Busovaca municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to block it, but to call the shots, I mean, to say yea or nay as to whether humanitarian aid could pass. And to charge rent, sometimes the UN had to pay for the use of their own road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that during the tours of duty of the three British battalions that served in central Bosnia; that is, from roughly November, 1992 until past October of 1993, every single UNHCR aid convoy that reached the BRITBAT area of responsibility reached its destination; do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about all, but certainly the vast majority, yes. I mean, they didn't appear to be taking much nonsense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall writing an article published in the Guardian on April 2, 1996 and which is attributed to you in which you wrote, or it is reported and written that you wrote, "In November, 1993 the Yorkshires left, the reckoning undisclosed. It is now estimated that between 40 and 50 Croats and 20 to 30 Muslims fell to the regiment's guns, an unbeaten UNPROFOR record, but every single UNHCR aid convoy that entered the Yorkshires' terrain reached its destination, a record shared only with the Cheshires. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, that sounds right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that the conflict in Prozor in October of 1992 would have heightened tensions between Croats and Muslims in central Bosnia; that is, in the Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak municipalities, that the nearness and proximity of that open conflict in Prozor would have heightened tensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Let's get back to the question from the Bench. I mean, 'open conflict', I mean, this was a bombardment of a civilian population that left town. The Croats didn't leave Prozor, the Muslims did. That is bound to increase tensions in central Bosnia, yes. How could it not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you become aware, directing your attention to Exhibit 29L, of a point in time following October, 1992 when the BiH army came to control portions of the terrain over which Route Diamond passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you give me the dates again, sir? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point in time after the HVO came to control the town of Prozor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Did you learn that the BiH army had taken control over some portion of the terrain between Prozor and where Route Diamond enters central Bosnia proper via Novi Travnik or Travnik? Did you become aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I was aware of it. At some point further up you went through BiH army checkpoints. There was one in Novi Travnik as you came around a short bend, if I recall, and the Bosnian army also controls a forest up above Gornji Vakuf which was also along Route Diamond.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And above that forest; that is, the forest above Gornji Vakuf, could the BiH army shell the road and essentially close it to Travnik, if they wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could, and both sides could and did shell it in Gornji Vakuf itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, roughly, when this was that Route Diamond came under the control of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, the area to the north of that forest was always in their hands I think, or if it wasn't, then, you know, then I would have been out of the country. So I'm not quite sure that there was -- I mean, there were bits of Route Diamond further up towards Vitez which, I'm trying to think, which they had -- which the BiH army had from October and had not lost in October and kept, I think, into 1993, probably held until about February, 1993 when I think they then lost the roadblock that I talked about on the bend in the road. I wish I had a village. I don't know, I'm afraid. You come out of the forest, you go down towards Novi Travnik, you come to a bend in the road, there was a BiH checkpoint there and it had gone by January 1993 so they had had it up until then, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that at other point or points or Route Diamond after February 1993, the BiH army maintained its positions and control over some portion of Route Diamond up until the Washington Agreement in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in July 1993, I can't answer the question, actually, because in July 1993, the fighting was so heavy on Route Diamond that it was unusable. As I said, you had to use the other route through. Sorry, that was February 1993 when we got knocked back. July 1993, I didn't see a BiH army checkpoint when I went on Route Diamond in 1993, but that's not to say they didn't control some of the area in the forest where they may not have had checkpoints because there was a gang up there that people didn't want to meet, but they didn't have checkpoints but we were told that the Bosnian army still controlled parts of the forest, but I'm afraid I can't help you with specific roadblocks. I don't think there were any by the time we got to July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in summary, this will be my last question, as far as you know, at all relevant times after -- from October 1992 to the Washington agreement, the BiH army had the ability to cut off Route Diamond; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I honestly can't tell you all the way through. I mean, I didn't travel Route Diamond all the time right up until the Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the witness can finish his answer before counsel interrupts with another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll answer it as best I can. There were parts of Route Diamond that the BiH army definitely controlled up until January 1993 because they had checkpoints. There were parts of Route Diamond which they were reported to control in July 1993, but there were no visible checkpoints, but they may not have had any or they may have been in the forest. I can only really help you up until the summer of '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thereafter you don't know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thereafter, I don't know. I have to be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, how long do you think your cross-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about halfway through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I suggest that we have a five to ten-minute recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please? Mr. Hayman, I have discussed with my colleague, we are going to sit until quarter past one so as not to break up your cross-examination and we will resume at 2.30. Is the accused here? We can proceed without a transcript, almost without an usher, but without you we can't do anything, but we do need the accused. (The accused entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, let me turn your attention to the fall of Jajce. Was that in late October, 1992 that Jajce fell to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and going into the first days of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you testified that the fall of Jajce during that period of time led to an exodus of roughly 40,000 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of those were combatants but the majority were civilian refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were most of the refugees Croat or Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority -- 50/50, maybe slightly more Muslims, but a larger proportion of Croats than among the refugees that we had been talking about earlier coming from the Prijedor area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those refugees also flood into Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified earlier that some soldiers with whom you spoke said they had withdrawn from Jajce as part of a Croat-Serb deal. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that, and I recall them saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss that issue with the brigade commanders of both the HVO and the BiH army at the time in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they did not -- as I recall, they did not share that view. Both the HVO and the Bosnian army thought that the defence of Jajce had become untenable. The talk of a deal and the umbrage of it came from the troops themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree that the following statements were made, and I'm reading from an article attributed to you in the Guardian dated November 2, 1992. Colonel Haso Ribo of the Bosnian army, who has within a month changed from a genial and confident man into the lachrymose commander of a desperate army said, “We were under intense and irresistible military pressure pure and simple. There was the risk that Jajce would be cut off, the corridor cut by winter and that there would be a massacre." Do you recall Colonel Ribo making, in substance, that statement to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I recall the corridor up which he and his Croatian allies were trying to defend Jajce. We tried to get up it ourselves. It was absolutely terrifying. That was his position and, as I recall, the HVO had roughly the same argument. The different account was coming from the soldiers who had been defending the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall Colonel Filipovic of the HVO in Travnik telling you, at the same point in time, "It was an unequal battle and it became more and more so. The order to withdraw came from local civil authorities with tacit approval of both commands."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this. As I said, I think the HVO agreed with Commander Ribo -- Commander Filipovic agreed with Commander Ribo that they could no longer defend Jajce up this narrow corridor and that's what they said and that's what the men were saying. They were saying different things and I reported them both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In substance, did Colonel Filipovic make the statement to you that I made to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, in an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a checkpoint at Romboci (phoen) south-west of Prozor which you visited in October of 1992 where, at one point in time, there were soldiers wearing HOS uniforms and later those soldiers were wearing HVO uniforms. Do you recall that subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes, I went through that roadblock many, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you agree with the following statement on that general subject in your book at page 214, which reads: "That for a considerable period of time, the region was a lawless embroilment of militias fighting their own wars against each other amid what would become a bedlam of violence." And this is a reference to the Croat side I believe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a reference to the Mostar area in August, 1992 when there was an internecine row going on between the HOS and the HVO and, indeed, the HOS leader was killed by the HVO. That was at a time, indeed, when there was a melee of militias of various kinds, to a greater or lesser extent, under HVO command. That was some months before the period we were talking about back in August, 1992 and pertained to Mostar as I think is clear in the book, and it's a chapter called the Rule of Madness, I believe. The, if you like, imposition of HVO authority happened subsequent to that, and so far as I could see was pretty much in place by the time we got to this October watershed, if you like. But that's correct as regards to the Mostar area back in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony is then that things had changed by description in your book by roughly October, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had changed dramatically, yes, and would change in the weeks to come, yes, that the smaller units, the free-booters, or whatever we want to call them, were being marshalled under the top-down authority of Mate Boban and the HVO and that, by the time we get to the end of October, visibly at least, this more homogeneous authority, more monolithic authority is pretty much in place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any specific information you can share with the court concerning the way in which HOS units or a HOS unit in the Vitez municipality was absorbed into the HVO; that is, whether they came under the command of the operative zone, or whether they had a line of command as a special unit to the Ministry of Defence in Mostar? Do you have any specific information on that subject to provide to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't. I don't know about the HOS in Vitez specifically. This HOS unit that was manning the roadblock at Romboci (phoen) we got to know because they had a roadblock and you had to present yourselves to them and it had HOS written on the side of their little hut. And the HOS uniform was a full black tunic back in August. They didn't have that, they would have maybe fatigues, trousers and a black T-shirt. They came under HVO authority and had HVO uniforms in that last or penultimate week in October. I'm afraid I can't help you with HOS in Vitez. There were other groups in Vitez that we heard about who were coming under the command of the HVO. I'm not saying the HOS wasn't in Vitez, they may very well have been, but I didn't have any direct contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the thesis that the first truly high intensity, violent conflict between Croats and Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina was in Prozor in roughly October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first systematic driving out of Muslim civilians -- the first systematic attack upon the civilians by an army was in Prozor in 1992 -- in October, 1992 so far as I could see. You're using the term 'fighting' as though it was between two rival armies. I saw the aftermath of 5,000 civilians being shelled and shot out of a town and a subsequent looting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would agree that what happened in Prozor was at an intensity that had not happened anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina between Croats and Muslims at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the first ethnic cleansing, not a term I like and, with hindsight, a sort of scale model, a dry run, if you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also agree that that type of high intensity conflict between Croats and Muslims first came to the Vitez Busovaca and Kiseljak municipalities in the municipality of Busovaca in January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez, Kiseljak and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, in the Vitez and Kiseljak enclaves, did the first intense conflict come in the Busovaca municipality in January of 1993? Would you agree that that is true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Busovaca and Stari Vitez, I'm not sure which would have been the first, but they would have been the first two, yes. Kiseljak had very few Muslims living there, so obviously the intensity was lesser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement in your book at page 255 that, "at Busovaca, in the Lasva Valley, it was the armija which came down from the hills and "cleaned" out the Croatians." Would you agree with that statement in your book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the village is just to the east of Busovaca, yes. I'm not trying to say that this is all one-way traffic. It's pretty obvious who has got the upper hand, it's the HVO, but I'm not here to pretend that this is all one-way. Yes, the Muslims were attacking as well. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the village is to the east of Busovaca, are you referring to Dusina and Lasva, or are you referring to Gusti Grab and Oceust down between Kacuni and Bilalovac; can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the area at the south-east at which the BiH army set up a roadblock shortly after that time. I don't want to get into a conversation about specific villages, because if I did I would then be going beyond by specific knowledge which I don't want to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you understand, by that roadblock, cutting the main road from Busovaca to Kiseljak; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For awhile, yes, the BiH army had a roadblock south of Busovaca on that road to Kiseljak, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also describe the ensuing conflict in and around Busovaca as follows: "The squalid small-town nature of the violence led to the rapid circulation of rumours which in turn fanned the flames of fighting". Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's return to Travnik and Colonel Filipovic, the HVO commander you've described meeting. I believe you visited him in January, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Colonel Filipovic would have none of Boban's war with the BiH army. Could you tell us, again, briefly how did he exhibit his desire to cooperate with the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With an episode that I described in my testimony. At considerable risk to himself and his opposite number in the BiH army and us, I might add, we went up Mount Vlacic together, so within a few hundred yards of the Serb guns, and he staged a little sort of filmed episode at which he sat next to his opposite number in the BiH army, Commander Kulilovic and made it clear that -- they joked a bit about how at least we can tell each other we don't trust each other, and then he made this remark that, yes, I'm walking the edge of the knife. I mean, that was his way of saying I'm very unhappy about this, and a rather potent way it was too, under the guns up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that Colonel Filipovic made no attempt to hide his active cooperation with the BiH army, rather, he attempted to promote and publicise his views in that regard. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wanted to say, I think, if I interpret him properly, that as he put it, "coming up the valley towards Travnik was a pressure on him to adopt a bellicose attitude towards his Muslim allies and that he didn't want to do that; and he was, as you say, yes, I agree with you, he was making it quite clear that he didn't want to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was publicising -- actively publicising those views; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversation with him when he said he was being made to walk the edge of the knife, was this on your trek up the Vlacic feature and how long was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was intermittent and having to split up, you don't know when you're approaching a gun position, you have to stretch apart and it was either on the way up -- actually, it was more than likely when we were sitting on the rocks under the guns or on the way down. We spent some time together to wait for a truck to meet us by sort of a hut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he expressly say what he meant when he said he was being made to walk the edge of the knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, he did. He talked about pressures coming up the valley. That is when I heard Colonel Blaskic's name mentioned and Mate Boban. He was articulate about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say Colonel Blaskic was making him do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Walk the edge of the knife, which I took to mean tightrope walk between two things he didn't want to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time Colonel Filipovic was actively promoting cooperation with the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say what it was Colonel Blaskic was ordering him to do what he didn't want to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he didn't specify. He grouped Colonel Blaskic together with Mate Boban and said that he was walking the edge of the knife, they were making him walk the edge of the knife, and that he wanted to -- that he -- I took that to mean, and by all means try an alternative interpretation if you want, there were two things he didn't want to do, he didn't want to leave the HVO because he was an HVO man and a Croat and a loyal Croat, but nor did he want to do that he was pressurised to do, which was to adopt hostile attitude to the BiH army that was happening almost everywhere else across the territory, apart from Travnik and places to the north and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree from the conduct that he exhibited and, indeed, promoted, that he had not been forced to adopt and exhibit any type of hostile attitude towards the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He made it clear that he was under extreme pressure to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he attack the BiH army in Travnik in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how long he remained the commander during that spring, so I would be -- I don't want to -- I'd like to help, but I don't want to make any suppositions. There was fighting later that spring, but I wasn't there and I wouldn't want to testify as to how it started or who started it or whether he was still the commander. I'm afraid I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is your understanding that ultimately in the spring or June, approximately, of 1993, it was the BiH army that drove the HVO out of Travnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, have you kept in touch with General Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were aware that he was promoted to the rank of General within the HVO; weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew he had been promoted. I didn't know he was a General and then I can only presume that he went over that side of the knife and not the other side. I don't think he wanted to fall on it, nor do I blame him. But, no, I haven't kept in touch with him is the answer, but I respected his position. I thought he was a decent man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man committed to his views; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, a man who believed in the alliance between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please face the Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: When you get the question, I say this to all the witnesses, of course, it is normal your question comes from one side or the other and it is normal that you turn that way; but when you're answering, please, address the Judges because, after all, they are there for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall, I'm sorry. He was a man who, so far as I could gather, believed in the alliance at the beginning of the war between the Bosnian army and the HVO, as was planned we thought, wrongly, and it is for that that I respected him. We had seen a horrific amount of the violence that the Serbs had meted out to both people and, as a group of journalists covering the war, and I suppose to say we hoped that alliance would hold together as well and it didn't. It was refreshing when you met Croats who believed in it and were prepared to speak their mind against this command from on high. I thought he was doing something honourable by trying, at least, if not successfully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In sum, you found him to be a man of honesty and integrity; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The Croats and the Muslims had been fighting together against this juggernaught of violence that the Serbs were meting out to their people, and we had seen that in alliance in Mostar, they were effective against all the odds, and here was Mate Boban and his command structure rupturing that alliance, and here was a man who was not prepared to administer a knife in the back and I admired him for it. He was against the run of play and he was a brave man for doing so. What happened to him after that, as I've said, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If Exhibit 173 could be put on the easel, I'll ask you a few preliminary questions first while it's being put on the easel. You left Bosnia-Herzegovina in February of 1993 and did not return until July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July of 1993, you did visit the Vitez area; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I believe you said in your earlier testimony that during that visit to Vitez in July of 1993 it came to your attention, rather dramatically, that there was a sniper of the BiH army firing on the garden in the home in which you were staying from a hill next to the British battalion headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you take a look at Exhibit 173, which is the smaller aerial photograph -- perhaps it will fit on the ELMO, I apologise. Why don't we try that? I apologise to the usher for that needless effort. And my question for you, Mr. Vulliamy, would be: Can you indicate on Exhibit 173 the hill from which this Bosnian army sniper fired on the residence in which you were staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I shall try. I only later learned he was in the Bosnian army, actually. His flag up there was the crescent, the Islamic crescent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can orient the map the other way so the numbers are facing the bottom of the screen; in other words, a quarter turn in a counter-clockwise direction, I believe. Now, if it could be lowered on the ELMO -- the other way, the other direction, please, a little bit lower, please, just another inch or two lower. Thank you. First of all, on Exhibit 173, Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise the area below the letter '1', not in the circle that is marked 1, but below the letter'1', the large number of light-coloured buildings? Do you recognise that as constituting all or parts of the BRITBAT base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate whether the hill from which this-- where was the hill, where was the approximate location of the sniper that was firing on you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm trying to find what was known as television alley which is where the BBC had a house, television as it was jokingly called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To help you orient further, do you see the bridge, see the river or the stream and the bridge going over the river and the stream just above the number 3A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then as you go up the photograph to 4A and 4, that is a hill frequently referred to as Grbavica. Does that help you orient yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A bit, yes. I'm trying to find the house first and, as soon as I've got the road and the house, I'll know exactly where the hill is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this is the television alley, as it was called, either that or that, and the -- yes, that's right. So we're here and the garden is here and he's been shooting down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can't see anything now, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I believe we can't cover that portion of the ELMO, Mr. Usher, because as we cover that upper portion of the ELMO we're obstructing the workings of the ELMO itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, on the lower portion of Exhibit 173, can you tell us-- ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, is this the main road here? This is where the houses were that the BBC would have been in. Do you happen to know that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My understanding, and the Prosecutor can disagree if he so wishes, is that the road you indicated is the main road going by the BRITBAT base. And the top of the photograph is the portion of the road heading in an east or south-easterly direction and the portion on which you have the pin now is the portion of the road heading west/north-west, away from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. Well, in that case, that's television alley, as it was called, and the garden is somewhere there, and if that's the hill, the sniper would have been shooting behind the BRITBAT into the garden. So the sniper was located approximately at the circle marked 4 on Exhibit 173; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so. I have to say -- if anyone can help me find television alley, I hate to use the term, but that's what it was called, then I will be able to mark the hill with more accuracy, but the house was -- the house ran adjacent to the main road behind the BRITBAT and the hill was to the west of the house. And so the snipers firing on us it would have come behind the BRITBAT which would be in that direction. So I'm prepared to say that that is the hill. If that is the road, if I'm right in identifying in the road, and I think I am find the road, then you're right in identifying the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We're concluded with that exhibit, Mr. Usher. You described your visit also to east Mostar in July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No visit to east Mostar in July, 1993, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later then in time you visited --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: September, 1993 first time in east Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good, thank you for correcting me. Did you learn during that visit or any other visit what the size of the BiH army unit or units were in east Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't learn the exact size. I mean, they were there. They were very scantily armed. It certainly wasn't - to refer us back to our previous conversation - this was not fighting. It was enclosed, it was fully enclosed. There was a small track coming down from Lepenice that you could get ammunition in through horseback, but apart from that it was completely cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were under siege; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And how, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of the number of BiH army soldiers in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. But the number of soldiers is almost irrelevant. I mean, there were plenty of soldiers with maybe a couple of bullets each, I don't know. But east Mostar was -- when you say 'under siege', yes, indeed. There were four-figure numbers of shells and mortars coming in every day exploding and killing and maiming a population swelled with women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether civilians were invited to leave east Mostar at any occasion -- on any occasion during the siege?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony at page 7789 that you concluded from events in October of '92 that there was one chain of command under Mate Boban and that it was working. Do you have any specific information for the Tribunal concerning the way in which Mate Boban exerted control over HVO military units; that is, did he issue orders through HVO military commanders? Did he issue orders through HDZ political channels? How did he exert control, as you have concluded, over the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can say what I saw at Mate Boban's various headquarters, which was that there were never not senior HVO people there. I mean, the HVO were always in his company. He talked of the HVO as though it were the executor of what he intended to carry out. He would talk about the HVO a lot more than he talked about the HDZ, of which he was the official. I mean, he used HDZ, HVO, almost interchangeably and was forever asserting to us the authority of the HVO throughout the territory. That is what I got from being with him and being at his headquarters. When it comes to what one saw happening, what I saw happening on the ground, then I can say that everything that Mate Boban said he was going to do was then done by the HVO. If he said, you know, we are now going to assert our authority in this way, as he did in that meeting I had with him in October, we could see it happening all over the territory, in Vitez, in Mostar (inaudible) with mobilisations on the road accordingly. This was more than anecdotal. So that's my answer. Two things: One is what you saw and the people you saw at Mate Boban's headquarters, and the way he talked about the HVO. I mean, he didn't say, I hope the HVO will do this; he said, the HVO will do this. And then the second part of the answer, on the ground, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid you misunderstood my question and answered a different question. My question was--

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to counsel's comments. If counsel has another question, he can ask another question. The editorialising, I think is objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The record is clear. The answer was not responsive and the court can take notice of that, and I think I should be permitted to refocus the witness on the question so we can get an answer to it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The answer is the answer to the question that was given. This is the witness' answer. If counsel doesn't like that answer, that's another subject, but counsel's editorialising on responses to the questions is improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Kehoe, but it didn't sound to me like a commentary. It didn't seem to me to be as particularly weighty or substantial but, in any case, we need a little rest, so I suggest that we adjourn. The witness will also be able to take a breather, and we will resume at a quarter to three. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.13 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, as all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Vulliamy, I have three or four or areas to cover, if you will bear with me. I'm nearing the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine. Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we broke before lunch, the question I was trying to express and ask was, is it correct that you were not privy to the types of internal communications with either the HVO or the HDZ that would shed light on what orders were issued, to whom they were issued, through what chains or lines of commands they were issued vis-à-vis Mr. Boban and others in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. The HVO were not showing me, or, to my knowledge, anybody else, their internal commands, nor was Mr. Boban, so I wasn't privy to their classified documents. What I was not privy to but witness to, were Mr. Boban's declarations of intent as regards both the HDZ and the HVO, and the way in which he regarded both as on hand and available to him to carry out his intentions, and those intentions accordingly being carried out as sequiturs on the ground, so one didn't need to see the internal documentation. You just had to see what they were doing to people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were his intentions in the municipality of Travnik, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, his intentions in the municipality of Travnik, was that Travnik, despite its northern position and its Muslim majority should be part of Herceg-Bosna. That was declared and that -- well, quite what being part of Herceg-Bosna entailed was made manifest to us from what ensued in Prozor, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Mostar and other places, namely, as I tried to say earlier in my testimony, one came reluctantly to the realisation that no Muslims were meant to be living in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion is that, Boban intended, that all Muslims were to be driven out of the Travnik municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think Mate Boban wanted the population of Herceg-Bosna to be as much -- to be as exclusively Croatian as possible and that if Muslims were intended to remain within that territory, they were to have professed -- they were to be sufficiently subservient to his order, further to present no threat. I'm not saying that he wanted a complete, sort of, Muslimised statelet, but I'm saying that he certainly did not intend to have any Muslims in the area under his command who were going to present him with any kind of political military problem, as he saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Putting the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Travnik was part of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Putting the incident at the gasoline station aside, and as to which you have already said you don't know whether there was a local history giving rise to that incident or not, but putting that incident aside, can you tell us anything the HVO did in Travnik in October 1992 to force the BiH army to come under the command or be subservient to the HVO. Did they do anything else, that you can tell the judges about in October 1992, consistent with the intent you have expressed on the part of Mate Boban, in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and that's precisely my point. Travnik, the HVO in Travnik, presented Mate Boban and the chain of command was developed or almost developed by October 1992, with a problem. The city had a tradition of tolerance between the two.
