It had been, and this was another important difference, I think, it had been a front-line town in the war against the Serbs, so there was an experience of fighting together among the soldiers of both sides, unlike, in many of the other places in Herzegovina, although not Mostar, I will agree, and yes, it was a central Bosnian town and it was more tolerant than most, and I think the HVO and Mate Boban had a problem in Travnik. In October 1992, that which Mate Boban was able to mobilise within the HVO behind his intentions at, as we saw, Prozor, Novi Travnik, Vitez, Mostar, he was not able to achieve in Travnik precisely because he could not get the commanders to fall into line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would agree that local events varied depending on the conditions, relationship between the HVO, and the BiH army and other local factors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. I would say there were exceptions to the rule and they were easily identifiable and they were isolated exceptions. One was Travnik. The other was up in Tuzla, where another tradition of tolerance existed and there were small villages in the area between Zenice and Tuzla, where the HVO declined to accept this hostile position as regards to the BiH army. I would not say that it was -- it was like sort of a jigsaw in which everyone made up their own mind. I'm talking about specific places where there were different traditions and specific commanders in place who sought to defy what was going on in Mostar, Vitez, Tomislavgrad, Prozor, Novi Travnik and, as it were, the main block of Herec-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me, HVO commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically in Travnik and Tuzla where the HVO -- in Travnik, I mean, it did come to blows in the end, although not quite as dramatically in Prozor and the other places, but Travnik was the one place, where the HVO sort of held out against this obligation on them coming up the valley, as Filipovic put it, to engage the Muslims in a war. And the other place was Tuzla which we haven't talked much about, which was way, way, to the north where the Croats remained loyal to the government army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And there was no massacres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zepca, do you know, in October of 1992, did the HVO adopt a hostile, an aggressive or a cooperative stand vis-à-vis the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I know, in Zepca, I never went to Zepca, it was cut off, but people came down into Travnik and Vitez from Zepca and, I don't know about October 1992, I'm afraid I can't answer your question, but later on in 1993, Zepca and Zavidovici which was a nearby village were reported to be, this is me reporting to you what I heard, two places where an infamous alliance between the HVO and the Serbs took place, and the HVO and the Serbs built a pontoon together bridge in that area to try and cut off the Muslims. You raised Zepca as an example. It was a particularly perfidious situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992 or the first half of 1993, do you know, did the HVO in Zepca adopt a cooperative stand vis-à-vis the BiH army or were they aggressive and hostile towards the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about 1992 but during the summer of 1993, as I said, in Zepca, the HVO was reported to join ranks with the Serbs against the Muslims. I'm repeating what I heard reported. I did not see this happen firsthand. (Witness please slow down).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if in Vares, to the north-east or east of Zenica, in October of 1992, the HVO adopted a cooperative stand vis-à-vis the BiH army or were they aggressive and hostile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vares was another that I should have added to the list that included Travnik and Tuzla, but in Vares something very sad happened. In Vares, which is just above Olovo in the eastern bit of central Bosnia, the HVO was, again, wanting to be cooperative with the Bosnian government army and they were themselves deposed during 1993 by other units of the HVO, who came up from Kiseljak to depose, get rid of, the elements in the HVO who had sought to cooperate with the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were the forces and units of Ivica Rajic that came up with Kiseljak and had effective control over Vares; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. The HVO in Vares had tried to cooperate with the alias, as Mr. Filipovic, of whom we've spoken in Travnik and, well, they were walking the edge of the knife as well, because Mr. Rajic's battalion's came up from Kiseljak and ousted those in Vares who were wishing to cooperate with the Bosnian army. That is another good example of the will of what was coming up the valley imposing itself against those who wished to cooperate with the Bosnian army, and that is quite well reported, that, again, sad putsch against Croats who wished to be -- take a more moderate position towards the government army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to summarise, in the fall of 1992, Vares was an exception to the thesis you've stated. Zepca was an exception and Travnik was also an exception; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and none survived. They were all either brought to heal or they, in the case of Travnik, the Muslims won out, as you've said before, and I agree. In the case of Vares, the moderates were opposed, pushed out and in Zepca, the indications were that they must have been pushed out because they were alive with the Serbs, by the summer of 1993, against the Muslims so, yes, in October, there was still -- I mean, the declaration that no dissent would be tolerated from Boban suggested there were dissent and that dissent was rubbed out. If you were still in the position of command, if you look at the pattern in the summer of 1993, those people were gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, of course, I omitted Busovaca where you've already said in January 1993 the BiH army attacked first. Wouldn't you include that in a way, the Busovaca municipality, as an exception to the thesis you've stated, given that the BiH army attacked first in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to be honest with you. I didn't know the HVO in Busovaca. I didn't hear that they were -- I certainly didn't hear that they were particularly moderate. My knowledge of the situation in Busovaca is that both sides were on for a war. I don't think the -- from what I've heard of Busovaca, I would not want to say, in a court, that they were among these moderates that I'm talking about, no, I've heard quite a lot about nastiness from both sides in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree that if the BiH army attacked the HVO first in January 1993, that is contrary to the basic thesis you have presented to this court and, thus, it would be appropriate to take Busovaca and hold it aside as somewhat of an exception to your thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the BiH army did attack first in Busovaca. I think in the town, the HVO attacked first. In the surrounding villages, the Muslims attacked with some unpleasantness. I know that the Muslims attacked in the villages to the south-east, because I saw the roadblock where they had taken a section of the road. I'm not trying to lily white those people. In the town, I don't know. I think it was tit or tat, probably. I wouldn't say that Busovaca was an exception. No, I don't think the HVO in Busovaca was attempting to defy the line in the way they were in Travnik, Tuzla is an exception, it's a long way off and it's not claimed by Herceg-Bosna, and as you remind me, Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an HVO unit in Zenica, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a small one, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that they had a cooperative relationship with the BiH army in the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I honestly don't know. I wasn't in Zenica at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have written, have you not, at page 258 of your book that Zenica was the "most stridently Muslim city in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By that, do you mean that by late 1992, the MOS, the Muslim armed forces composed of extremists and roughians had become more and more predominant in the city. I'm quoting from your book, at page 258? Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, as they felt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I don't mind if you cite the book of Mr. Vulliamy on two or three occasions, but please remain within the bounds of the examination-in-chief. I understand that it is important so I didn't want to stop you, but I still wouldn't like you to take too long. Up to now, it has been very logical, but to destabilise the witness, and I assume he is destabilised, should be prevented. I don't want us to spend the whole afternoon by extracting sentences from the book, seeing whether they are contradictory or not. We are here with a witness who said a certain number of things during his testimony on the 24th of April, 1998, so let us try and focus on what he actually said as much as possible. It is already at least five, six, seven times that you have cited this or that sentence from the book. In any case, I'm not here to defend the witness. I'm defending the judges. We are not at an institute of political relations. We have here a witness who testified on the 24th of April and you are now cross-examining him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would note I'm not speaking to destabilise the witness, but there are portions of his book that bear relationships to his thesis, and I thought it a quick and efficient way to confirm his views on certain points by referring him to the book. In fairness, cite from the book and give the Prosecutor the page so if they cared to explore it further on in their examination, they could. That’s all I was hoping to do. I'm moving as quickly as I can so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us then ask one question. Do you confirm your whole book? I'm going to ask you this question. Do you confirm what you wrote in your book? You wrote that book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 99.999 recurring percent of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then let us try to speed things up a little, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, you testified concerning the February 24, 1994 cease-fire and the fact that that cease-fire held throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Mostar at the time. As I testified, it certainly held remarkably there, and my testimony pertained to returning to Split and to find that colleagues had reported the same thing happening all over the place, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the first cease-fire ordered by General Petkovic since October 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were other cease-fires organised, but that was the first right across the board and certainly the one that worked. It was the first that held that I knew about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you remember any of the following cease-fires, and then if you know whether these cease-fires held and were successful. 21 October 1992 in Novi Travnik, 9 November, 1992 in Novi Travnik. 24 January, 1993 in Gornji Vakuf, 27, January 1993, operational zone central Bosnia. 30 January, 1993, operational zone, central Bosnia. 18 April, 1993, operative zone in central Bosnia between Boban and Izetbegovic, 20 April, 1993 in operational zone central Bosnia between Petkovic and Alilovic; 25 April, 1993 by Petrovic, 9 June, 1993 in Travnik between Alagic and Blaskic then 19, June, 1993 in operative zone, central Bosnia Blaskic, Hadjtasanovic. Do you know whether any of those other cease-fires held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some of them ring a bell, others don't. I know that after your last date, some of the most ferocious fighting was still to come. I don't know how long each particular one held. I remember the British UNPROFOR people used to count and have a record of the cease fires and made a joke about how little time they lasted. I believe 13 seconds was the record. But if you're talking about cease-fires, by definition, I think what you're mentioning are intervals. They do not and cannot have lasted because the war went on. Indeed, the very worst violence in Mostar, was to follow your last date, and so when I talk about the cease-fire in February 1994, I meant a cease-fire that was agreed and imposed and held to across the terrain, not some -- how shall I say it, some expedients which lasted a number of days, hours, sometimes. The war carried on through all the dates you've mentioned is what I mean, but some of them do ring a bell. In fact, I first heard Colonel Blaskic's name from a British army officer and someone from the UNHCR saying that they had been obliged to sign a cease-fire, that he had negotiated, and they were very uneasy about having to sign it. So yes, of course , I knew there were cease-fires but they didn't have any effect because the business wasn't finished.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that on the occasions on which cease-fires did not hold that we can conclude that if they did not hold on the side of the HVO, that on those occasions, the HVO chain of command failed to work with, I believe your words were, "coherence, cogency, and efficiency." Can we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we conclude that on the occasions on which cease-fires did not hold and were, indeed, violated by the HVO soldiers, that the HVO chain of command on those occasions did not work with "coherence, cogency, and efficiency," and I'm citing your description on page 7822 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll stick with my description, because I don't think that the cease-fires -- correct me if I'm wrong, I don't think all the cease-fires you're talking about are of the instructive weight of the Washington agreement. I mean, the point about the cease-fire on February 24th that I'm trying to make is that it was signed in Washington. The American diplomats had bargained it. The threat of sanctions was behind it and it was do it or else. These are -- in my experience, a lot of these cease-fires are expedient. Armies often agree a local cease-fire to move ammunitions around, to get a breather. I don't think that the crease-fires you're talking about were ordered by Mate Boban from Grude to be enforced permanently across the board and were broken by some rogue element. I think these were a hodgepodge of arrangements. I don't think that they were the same sort of cease-fire, like, stop firing, stop fighting, that happened in February '94. It was of a different nature, if I make myself clear. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more question on this subject and I'll move on. Are you saying that the orders for those cease-fires were not sincere by the commanders or politicians who issued them or are you saying that the stature of the Washington agreement with President Clinton of the United States and other international leaders validating the agreement, that it had a better chance of success than other cease-fires, and, indeed, with that additional weight, it was able to proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think that the witness has already answered, but please give us a very brief answer now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the intervals in fire, if you like, were often negotiated for expedient reasons, military reasons, and that the permanent cease-fire, the one that worked, was instructed by the chain of command going all the way up to Zagreb, in fact, and, as you say, had the force of American diplomacy behind it. It was stop fighting or else you're in big trouble. Everyone was threatening sanctions against Croatia when there was an operational cease-fire for a few hours in central Bosnia sometime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said in your testimony on direct that you read of an ultimatum issued by Bosnian Croats that the BiH army should come under HVO control or the HVO would implement the Vance-Owen peace plan. If the registrar could retrieve exhibit 25, so that it's handy should the witness need to reference it. Mr. Vulliamy, did you obtain any information concerning any such ultimatum, other than from reading a Reuters' report in your London office as you described on direct examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not at the time, no. It was reported in Reuters and it was reported on the radio as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you reviewed exhibit 25, which is another article discussing the subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that, but not at the time I wrote the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree, and if you don't know, that's fine, you can tell us, but would you agree that there's no deadline stated in that article or report for compliance with the terms of the Vance-Owen peace plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't recall, I don't want you to read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any specific information you can provide the court of any ultimatum issued or repeated by HVO authorities in the Lasva or Kiseljak valleys in April 1993 relating in any way to the subject matter of exhibit 25?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Counsel asked a question about a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel asked a question about exhibit 25 previously, and then when the witness wanted to read exhibit 25, counsel didn't want to take the time. Now he's asking about the content of exhibit 25, and if we're going to continue asking questions about this document, the witness should be given the opportunity to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, objection granted. Will you please familiarise yourself quickly with the document before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll read it as quick as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I may have to refer to it again, but I've got the gist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we've taken the time for you to read it, can you tell us, is there any deadline stated in the article for compliance with the terms of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There seems to be in item No. 2 on the list, on the second page a deadline for the gist of this document which seems to be, if you will forgive me for paraphrasing, you know, you get out of our territory and we'll get out of yours, of three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doesn't item 2, doesn't that refer to outside forces originating from outside the province or municipality in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think that's clarified later on as being that within the provinces that the Croats are claiming, or that are designated Croat, it's the HVO, and the BiH army would be considered an outside force and vice versa. So I suppose we're saying that you've got three days--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --for this mutually exclusive arrangement to come into effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be surprised to learn that the BiH army wanted that term because they wanted, for example, HVO units from Herzegovina out of central Bosnia just like the HVO wanted BiH army units from wherever, Tuzla, to withdraw themselves from central Bosnia? Would that surprise you? Your interpretation sounds to be very different from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would surprise me if the BiH army would want to agree to leave all the areas claimed by the HVO, yes, but then it's not really relevant what they think because towards the end of the document it goes on to say that if the Muslim delegations don't sign it, we're going to go ahead anyway. And then with reference to the Croatians, it goes on to say that anyone who does not agree should "now reduce their support to silence." So it doesn't really matter what anyone thinks, does it? They want it to happen anyway. And this is signed by Veso Vega who I came to meet in Mostar later, the main spokesman for the HVO in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other date or deadline, would you not agree, is point 4 which has a deadline for setting up a joint command between the HVO and the BiH army; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I don't understand, really, where that joint command is meant to be, if you could enlighten me, because it seems to me that we're having your bit and you're having yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Joint command, that doesn't sound very aggressive and hostile; does it? To set up a joint command, to want a joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, but it's very odd that they have been dismantling joint commands all this time. I don't know how long you want this argument to go on. Number 3 says that the HVO and the BiH army in provinces 1, 5, and 9, hardly any HVO in 1, 5 and 9, actually, very few, Tuzla is the biggest, shall be placed under the BiH army. 3, 8 and 10, which is Herceg-Bosna effectively, comes under the command of the main staff of the HVO. So I'm not quite sure what this joint command is supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think there's a question pending, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think there is, because Herceg-Bosna has come under the HVO. I mean, there's no argument about that. If the Muslims don't sign it, we're going to do it anyway, and if you're a Croat and you don't agree, you can "reduce your support to silence."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the deadline for item or term 3? Was there a deadline or was there no deadline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me have a look. You know this document better than I do, obviously. No, there wasn't a deadline for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my last question on this topic, I stated it previously, was objected to by counsel. I'll restate it. Regarding the subject matter of this alleged ultimatum, do you have any specific information to provide to the court concerning any ultimata issued or repeated by the HVO authorities in either the Lasva or Kiseljak Valleys in April -- in or around April, 1993 or do you not have any such specific information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. Mr. Vega speaks for the whole of the HVO in my experience, so such local adaptations wouldn't be necessary. And I've dealt with Vasa Vega, he is the main spokesman for the whole of the HVO, the top guy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have discussed the state -- excuse me. You have discussed the strategy of the HVO in purely offensive terms, as in offence versus defence. Would you agree that, in fact, the strategy of the HVO in the Vitez Busovaca pocket in 1993 was primarily defensive? Would you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two different phases. I can half agree. Vitez was, as I saw it, crucial to the HVO in two different ways at two different times of the period you're asking me about. It was crucial in the first stage, let's say late 1992 into '93, as you say, as the furthest reliable outpost of Herceg-Bosna. It was the northernmost bit of Herceg-Bosna in which Boban knew he could count on the HVO because of what we'll call the Travnik problem, for want of a better term. The further north the Croats got, the less -- or certainly north of Zenica, the less allegiance they owed to Mate Boban and his people down in Herzegovina. So Vitez was crucial to the HVO for the first bit of the period you're talking about as the uppermost reliable, the northernmost reliable bit, the bit on which Mate Boban could count, Vitez and Novi Travnik. At that stage, I would say its, the HVO's role in Vitez was very much offensive. Then, after what I'll call the backlash by the Muslims of the summer of 1993, Vitez, as you have said earlier on in your questions, ran the risk of being cut off from Herzegovina. It wasn't, actually, ever a complete pocket, but it became much less part of the Herzegovinian main chunk, if you like. At that point, Vitez was, if you like, I suppose even more important because there was this defensive element to the military operation. I mean, Vitez was under pressure during the latter part, the latter period that you say; whereas previously it had been offensive. I'm sorry to be complicated, but I agree with you, across the latter period there was a defensive ingredient, although there's nothing very defensive about a car bomb outside a Muslim enclave, which they blew up, as you know, killing a lot of civilians. But, yes, during the summer of 1993 the command of Vitez was equally crucial for reasons that were defensive as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did General Alagic tell you concerning the BiH army's offensive intentions with respect to central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alagic wanted to -- he saw the Muslims as being squeezed out and he wanted to establish -- in one of the conversations I had with him, he wanted to establish a triangle which would connect, as I recall, Tuzla, Sarajevo and Travnik, which would be sort of a Muslim triangle, and I think he saw that as a basis for fighting out, really, against Serbs and Croats from within that. That was one of the conversations I remember having with Alagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that strategy would involve displacing the HVO from the Lasva Valley; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine so, yes, frankly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the Lasva Valley was the critical communications link between Sarajevo and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how he saw -- I mean, at its media, if you like, which I'd say was probably late February, March 1993 when the Muslims really thought they were going to get stuck between a rock and a hard place, if you will pardon the expression, that was Alagic's own personal strategy. He wasn't commander of anything at that point, that was before he took command of what later became the 17th Krajina brigade, or otherwise known as or the refugee brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that the BiH army pursued that strategy with remarkable tenacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With a couple of minor geographical exceptions, yeah, I think they had to, and if -- I think they had to in order to survive. I think they were looking, as I've said, in a number of places, I think they were looking at extinction at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This brings me to my last question, Mr. Vulliamy. You interviewed Lieutenant Mark Jones of the 9th-12th Lancers Unit after the Ahmici massacre, and I believe he was in the first group of British soldiers to visit Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993. Did he tell you, "not a single Muslim house had been spared. Methodically and systematically, the hit squad went around the village blowing up at least 50 homes. It was a band of 15 to 20 gunmen high on slivovitz." I'm not suggesting the truth or the falsity of this statement, I'm simply asking you: Did he make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't do that interview, it was done by a colleague of mine who works for the Guardian called Ian Trainer (phoen). He did the interview and I think you got it from the book. It should be credited to the addition of the paper that I didn't write for. But he didn't tell that to me, he told it to a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Trainer a professional journalist on the staff of the Guardian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh absolutely, yes. He's at the moment our Berlin correspondent, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is slivovitz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a sort of plum -- it's plum brandy, a favourite of the soldiers in the area and of other people, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kehoe, you have some re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Related back to this last point, you have looked at what has happened in Ahmici -- directing your attention back to this last question by counsel for the Defence, you have looked at what's happened in Ahmici and you're aware of what has happened throughout the Lasva Valley, as in other places throughout Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: All of those events can be sourced back to groups of 15 to 20 gunmen who happened to be drunk on some kind of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've been trying to say throughout, I've been trying to say that we moved between Mate Boban and various commanders and what was happening on the ground. The war against the civilians accelerated as the political objectives, the military objectives became more articulate, and that what was going on, you could see -- you didn't even have to see the charred villages, you just had to look at the roads in between them, there was a mobilisation of an army going on. Yeah, there was a lot of slivovitz around as well, but not 15 or 20, no. There was units of soldiers, I mean, Prozors, units of soldiers. Vitez, Mostar was an entire army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counsel asked you questions about a series of meetings between Mate Boban and then some individuals in the field. Let's place those meetings in context. The first meeting counsel asked you about was in August of 1992 with Mate Boban where Muslims and the HVO had just driven the Serbs out of Mostar; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, about a month after they had joined forces in Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During that conversation, was Boban's hostility directed towards the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, to the government in Sarajevo, ergo as he called them, Muslims, yes, I mean, to my amazement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was that the conversation where Boban told you he could not accept a Bosnian constitution and that we are prepared to defend our freedom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, shortly after that, we discussed a conversation that you had with a commander in Travnik called Pokrajcic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Pokrajcic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, could it be fair to say -- and counsel asked you some questions about that Pokrajcic conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you said in response to questions by counsel that Pokrajcic was feeling some pressure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he told me about the pressure. In fact, the first I ever heard of tensions between Muslims and Croats was from the Croatian commander in Travnik, Mr. Pokrajcic, a young man, and he said he was feeling pressure and he didn't want to succumb to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you had this conversation with Mate Boban in the latter part of October of 1992, approximately a month or so after this conversation with Pokrajcic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the really important one I regarded as being.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, was that conversation more clear in the sense -- or clearer in the sense of what Boban wanted to happen in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it progressed to the same argument. I mean, the argument which was roughly sketched and, sort of, put in rather thinly veiled moderate language became robust, uncompromising and determined, articulate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You said in response to a question from Defence counsel that during that conversation, Boban deemed that he would not accept any dissent or people would have to leave in some other fashion if they decided to dissent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That there would be no dissent within the Croatian ranks and there would be no challenge to the hegemony of the HVO from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Would you say that pressure was part of the pressure that Filipovic was feeling in February of 1993 where he cursed Boban and the defendant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been trying to say. That was the pressure. When they are talking about pressure, I think we're sort of overanalysing this pressure. To me it's extremely obvious, and it still is that the pressure was on the people like Pokrajcic, the moderate Croat in Travnik, his successor Filipovic, the then moderate Croat in Travnik, that the pressure was to fight their allies and they didn't want to do it and the pressure seemed to be coming very obviously from Mate Boban and from the HVO to which they belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And in that conversation in October, Mate Boban told you that any deviation would not be tolerated; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, he said they would have to step down or be removed in some other manner, which is pretty menacing in the middle of a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the note of the 4th of April, 1993, Exhibit 25, the article by Veso Vega, that is to your left there, and the last half of the second page and over to the top of the third page, once again, Veso Vega on behalf of the HVO said that dissent should be silenced; doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that consistent with the conversation that you related on cross-examination with Mate Boban from October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it any surprise to you, in light of that conversation, that Filipovic made a decision to go with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't know he had been promoted but, yes, I said I admired the man, I can't blame him. I don't know what's happened to him since, yes, be removed in some other manner is a threat, and he obviously decided to batten down and obey his orders, probably to save his own skin, I should think, if not his career.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you conclude after that conversation with Filipovic and what you had known in your conversations with Boban, that the defendant Blaskic had agreed to go along with the ideas of Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It's beyond the scope, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was just asked numerous questions about this for about 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Rephrase your question, Mr. Kehoe, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You talked on cross-examination about the conversation with Mate Boban. You talked about the conversation in late February, 1993 with Filip Filipovic where he cursed the defendant Blaskic and Mate Boban. Did you conclude after that conversation -- with what you knew and what you saw, did you conclude that the defendant had agreed to go along with the ideas of Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Not only is this beyond the scope, this is an ultimate opinion not rendered on direct. He is going beyond what he said on direct. If it's allowed on re-direct, then there must be re-cross. That's my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence counsel just diced and spliced and tried to render these types of conversations that were discussed by this witness as unrelated in any fashion. In response to that line of questioning, the Prosecutor is entitled to allow this witness to complete what has been raised on cross-examination on these various meetings. That's all this is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Objection overruled. Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Will you answer the question, Mr. Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I understood from what Mr. Filipovic was telling me is that if you were someone who did not want to fight the Muslims, you were being put in an impossible position. That was the blade of the knife, you either fell off one side, which meant that you gave up your career, joined the Muslims or whatever; or, you fell off the other side which meant that you went along with this ghastly programme; or, I suppose, you did nothing and fell on the knife. I shan't not go into that. I think if you were a man like Filipovic you were faced with a very, very painful dilemma. And my answer to your question is, yes. I don't know what was going on inside Colonel Blaskic's head, but from what Mr. Filipovic was saying, it was clear to me that Boban -- it was coming up the valley. He said, it was coming from Boban, and Blaskic was mentioned in the same breath and that Blaskic was part of the pressure on him to turn against his Muslim allies, yes. And it did all come back to the conversation with Boban. It was hard to conclude otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On a separate subject, you were read a sentence by Mr. Hayman, and the sentence was from page 222, counsel. The sentence that was read was - and this has to do with the fighting in Prozor - "Then as dawn broke and people started to flee, mobs moved in to town firing willy-nilly and then began to torch, loot and cleanse the town." Do you remember being read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me read you the sentence before that. "HVO units had arrived from Tomislavgrad at the edge of Prozor on Friday evening and subjected the town centre and Muslim quarter to an all-night artillery barrage." Were the mobs that were discussed with you, were they HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniform and had, I mentioned the red ribbon tied to their epaulette. When I said we arrived after the firing and the looting, they arrived after the shelling and the shooting, but not -- and the looting was still going on. I think I said they were taking stuff out, and these were all uniformed soldiers, HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might have a moment to consult with my colleague. Mr. President, we have no further questions of Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we listened with great interest to your testimony. You made it clear that the ultimate goal of ethnic cleansing was decided and even articulated by the political leadership, Boban or whoever was around him, you made it very clear, sometimes you said that no Muslim was to remain in the area. And now, did also this political leadership prescribe the ways this ethnic cleansing should be done, or was it left to the judgement of every commander to proceed to the ethnic cleansing whether by transportation, or by killing, or by looting, or by burning? Was it also their directives or orders of the political leadership to proceed in this way according to your almost round experience there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed that there were variations, none of them pleasant. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There were variations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I said that no Muslims were to live in Herceg-Bosna, that was, you know, a conclusion that I drew from what I had seen in the shelling and shooting of people out of Prozor, and later Capljina empty of Muslims, men in camps, women and children herded into east Mostar. But I think if one could look at variance, in Mostar it was herd people out of their homes and send them across the river, bomb, shell and snipe them. In the area to the south of Mostar, the pattern was men into camps, and I think I mentioned this plan that they had discussed with the UNHCR for a mass deportation to third countries through a transit camp, while the women and children were herded into this small pocket in the eastern side of Mostar and subject to ferocious shell fire. In the Lasva Valley and around Prozor, it seemed to be a question of gun and some mortar attack followed by systematic torching of houses, chasing people out with a mixture of gunfire and the torching of houses. I mean, it was systematic in terms of the objective, but I really don't know who decided who was going to be torched, who was going to be put in camps, who was going to be sent to east Mostar and shelled. It wasn't -- it happened over a longer period of time then the Serb equivalent which happened in the Drina Valley in the east of Bosnia and around the Prijedor, Banja Luka area in 1992 where larger numbers of people were removed or detained in camps much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think you also in one of your statements said that Boban mentioned that the policy is decided by him, but the implementation is left to the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He said that -- he was talking about the representation at the Geneva peace talks at that point, and he said it will be myself, or those whom I delegate, or those whom you see in my company, he said, and no others. As regards the HVO, he talked more about the HVO as the sole authority and he sort of -- I mean, he described them, as had a lot of the other people, Skopljak in Vitez, Lasic and Mostar, as the sole legal authority in Vitez. The civilian military authority, were the words he used in Mostar. Boban talked about the HVO also as being the sole authority. I took that to mean that they were the executor of his political decisions. I mean, military wing was a word used earlier of the party. I'm not quite sure that was quite right. I think he basically saw Herceg-Bosna as a statelet, him as the head of state, and the HVO as the army. So just as the president of a country is the commander in chief of the armed forces, I think that was how he, in his rather self-grandiose way saw himself in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Within the HVO there was, as you said, a variation in the implementation of the policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the details, yes. One area, the emphasis seemed to be on shooting and mortar and burning out; in other areas, it was round men into camps, women and children elsewhere. Not a great deal of variation. It all had the same -- well, to me grotesque message to it, the same grotesque repulsion and motivation which was the systematic and violent removal of innocent and unarmed civilians from their place of dwelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Some areas were more enthusiastic than others in this procedure, this process of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. And some as I've tried to make clear, tried to avoid it all together, a few, Travnik, Tuzla and Vares didn't want any part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where would you situate the area of General Blaskic in this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the sort of comparative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Comparatively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, Mostar has to be said to be the worst, which was not in General Blaskic's area, I know. I mean, Mostar, the largest numbers were involved, the most ferocious cruelty involved in the camps were there. On the other hand, I think that -- Ahmici rates pretty high on the horror list. I think there was - and I didn't see this so I have to rely on colleagues and newspaper reports - but there was one body exchange in Vitez, apparently, which a colleague of mine reported and said it was a pitiful sight. The Muslims got to hand back four Croatian bodies and the Croats handed back some 92 bodies, some of them child size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vitez. There was a famous incident of a car bomb placed right at the edge of the Muslim quarter of Vitez which killed a large number of civilians. It's hard to, as during my testimony I sort of tried to avoid this comparative thing, but I think one has to. The Lasva Valley, not quite the zeal of Mostar, not quite the violence of Mostar, and to my knowledge, no camps like Dretelj, but let the court make what it will of body exchanges 90 to 4. I don't think that's challenged, including children among the 90. The car bomb in Ahmici. It's not far down the scale of barbarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One clarification also. When you were mentioning Boban's position with regard to HVO and the HDZ, you said one did not need to see the internal documentation, but just to see what they were doing to people. What do you mean by internal documentation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was asked a question by Defence counsel about had I seen any internal orders, I think that was the idea, had I seen specific instructions to specific commanders. The answer is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, instructions from Boban to the commanders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I took that to be the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's what you meant by documentation. Not instructions from the commanders to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Which one did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see either instructions from Boban to the commanders or from the commanders to the soldiers, so I wasn't privy to any of the internal documentation and I don't pretend to be. What I meant was, if you see peoples' houses bombed and shelled and burned out and people sort of running around hiding in caves from soldiers who are out to hunt them down, I sort of -- to make a personal point, I'm not sure I need to see the orders if I'm seeing this. In a way, this tells me everything I need to know about what the orders must have been. Likewise, in Mostar, do I need to see the HVO orders if I'm running around the street being shot at and watching shells being pumped into a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mean it speaks for itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me it does when you see it happening day after day, week after week, month after month, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So it was done in an organised systematic way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see how else it could have been done because of the -- well, because of the speed with which it ignited at the end of October and, most especially, I referred to this in the testimony, the extraordinary speed with which it was switched off on the 24th of October, or whenever it was, of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mean it was all under control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, if this had been a hodgepodge of free booting drunken militias, you would not have been able to have had war in Vitez, war in the Lasva Valley, war in Vares, and an almighty great siege - siege is too clean a word - slaughter in east Mostar, going on on the 23rd of February and then nothing on the 24th of February without orders being given and obeyed. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Two or three clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand that you do not count Mr. Boban among the moderate Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Through those conversations, were you able to assess whether General Blaskic would be one of the moderate Croats or, due to his position of command, does that mean that he could not have been a moderate Croat in view of the level of responsibility that he had? Of course, through the conversations that you had with Mr. Boban, I'm not asking you for an opinion, but what you concluded on the basis of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I can say, we've spoken enough about the conversation with Colonel Filipovic. I don't need to return to it, unless you want me. As regards the conversations with Mr. Boban, he never mentioned Colonel Blaskic by name to me, but there was no -- I mean, Vitez was important to him and he talked about Vitez, but he didn't mention Mr. Blaskic by name. So I think it would be array of me to try and read into his view of Colonel Blaskic. I don't think that would be proper. Certainly to remain in a position of authority in an important military area -- and defence counsel has -- we've discussed how important Vitez was, both offensively at the beginning of the project, and then defensively once the backlash started. I think, you know, one would presume that Colonel Blaskic was certainly trusted with the command of a crucial area. It would not have made sense, given the second conversation with Mr. Boban in which he talked about no dissent being tolerated, it would not have made sense for a dissenter to have stayed that long in such an important area, and nor would it make sense for him to be some sort of ceremonial figure and he comes out for the saluting of the flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Regarding the cease-fires, Mr. Vulliamy, you said that there were many. You gave us a list, together with Mr. Hayman, but there was some that, to you, were real cease-fires. I'm caricaturing a little bit what you said, and then others that couldn't hold. Anyway, my question is: Within this long series of cease-fires, did you have a feeling that some were concluded in full responsibility by Mate Boban and Colonel Blaskic? That's the first part of my question. And the other part is, that they were broken by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that some of the cease-fires were concluded by Mr. Boban, and I know that directly one of them was concluded by Colonel Blaskic, because of the unease of the British army officer I mentioned who was asked to sign that particular cease-fire which, I think, would have been at the end of 1992, although I'm not sure which one exactly would have been on the list that Mr. Hayman read. Yes, I didn't know about all those cease-fires. I knew that cease-fires were declared for prisoner exchanges quite often, that when prisoners were crossing the front-lines, these were very frequent, each side would negotiate a temporary cease-fire to allow for the transfer of prisoners. Such cease-fires were also very useful to us to go up onto the front-lines where the Serbs were concerned, because they would happen across Turbe, and it was the only way he could get close to the Serb lines during these cease-fires. But I think we're confusing the word "cease-fire" here a bit. When I said cease-fire, you said kindly that there was one or there was some that I can't -- I mean, really only one. I mean, there were intervals in fire arranged locally for a number of reasons, and I wouldn't presume to explain each of the ones on Mr. Hayman's list, but often reinforcements, or maybe with good intent locally occasionally, but in my experience, with some other agenda, prisoner exchange being a common one. The cease-fire I'm talking about in February, 1994 was a cessation of hostilities. That's what I call a cease-fire, is when people stop firing. All the dates in the list we had earlier were followed by terrible violence and, no, I'm not able to, I'm afraid, comment on specific cease-fires being broken by General Blaskic. I just simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you able to identify through your conversations political, institutional and military links between Mate Boban and Croatia within the framwork of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fairly frequent. Sometimes these were anecdotal, inasmuch as there were very often buses loaded with armed men coming up from Split, and the Adriatic coast up into the Mostar area in particular, and occasionally up through Tomislavgrad into central Bosnia. Perhaps most conclusively during the siege of Mostar, when I got to know a Danish UNMO, a United Nations military observer, an official, who made it his particular business to identify the tanks that were being used to shell east Mostar, and he told us that a lot of the T-55, some of the older tanks were HV tanks, Croatian army proper, rather than HVO. And there was a story also earlier on, and I remember reporting this earlier, in Zagreb that there was at one point a battalion of the HV fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina with the Bosnian Croats. Apart from that, as regards to Mr. Boban himself, no; apart from his obvious affection for and tie to and natural affinity with Croatia, and that he was in Croatia a lot. The border, I've said before, was a sieve as well, I mean, it was a very cursory border. It had a Bosnian army guard at the crossing points up until about October, 1992; after which there was no sign of any Bosnian presence at the border post. It was all Croat and Bosnian Croat. As I say, a lot of military toeing and froing across the border on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Another question, Mr. Vulliamy. In answer to a question by my colleague, you said that Mostar held the first place for the conflict we are concerned with. Do you have the impression that the high staff -- for the high staff for the politicians, Mostar was an example that need to be followed, or as something to be rejected, too heavy a price to pay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I mean, Mostar was dearest to the hearts of the Herceg-Bosna project. It was to be the great capital. Mate Boban said that it was the only city that has a university, an airport and industry, and I think the HVO was prepared to fight more bitterly and to the end for Mostar, than perhaps for any other single bit of the envisaged territory. Mostar was certainly not supposed to be something to be reacted against. I think it was the summation of it all, really; nor could it be seen to be a model because it sort of built up to a crescendo towards the end. The worst of the Mostar siege was from August, 1993 until February, '94, so it came at the end, if you like, you know, temporally of the line. So, I mean Mostar as that which the HVO would not give up at any cost, yes, I think that was certainly a model that the rest of the statelet was supposed to follow. Mostar is sort of shining star, if you like. But certainly I don't think that it as something that the rest of Herceg-Bosna was supposed to be -- to learn a lesson of warning from. I didn't at all get the impression that the people in Tomislavgrad or Vitez or Kiseljak were supposed to look at the bloody siege of Mostar and think, mustn’t do it like that. No, not at all. I think it was a sign of the HVO to get what it claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. You have come on several occasions and, on behalf of the Tribunal, I must apologise to you for these various inconveniences. You have shown a great deal of patience and you have contributed to the Tribunal important testimony, and all the parties here present will draw from that testimony. I think that you have finished in principle, so allow me to convey to you our gratitude. You will not move for the time being. We're going to adjourn for a 20-minute break, roughly. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Can you bring in the accused? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, at this point, we will start the cross on Witness NN. I would say that there were protective measures for Witness NN, who testified at the latter part of last week on Friday. One of those protective measures was voice distortion. I've been informed, Mr. President and Judge Riad, that voice distortion is not possible in this courtroom with the equipment available. Accordingly, I've discussed this with counsel for the defence, and the Prosecution would ask that we go into closed session for the cross-examination of Witness NN because of the unavailability of voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Well, of course, necessity makes the law in all parts of the world, so we shall proceed in that manner. Mr. Hayman has also stated his view, so, Mr. Usher, we shall have a closed session and we shall ask the usher -- how do we proceed? Do we know is it enough to empty the fourth booth on the right? I don't know if there was anyone in that booth? Were there some spectators? Please proceed with a security officer sitting there. (Closed Session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 12th day of May, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
